newsitem.title: UZBEKISTAN: Uzbeks seal ex-Soviet frontier with Afghanistan.
newsitem.headline: Uzbeks seal ex-Soviet frontier with Afghanistan.

text.p: The former Soviet republic of Uzbekistan closed the only crossing on its Afghan frontier on Wednesday as a precaution against fighting in northern Afghanistan involving the Taleban militia.

Even travellers with visas were not allowed to pass the checkpoint at Friendship Bridge near the Uzbek town of Termez. The bridge carries the main Kabul highway north over the Amu Darya river, once known as the Oxus, into what used to be Soviet territory.
Only several foreign aid workers leaving Afghanistan were allowed to cross into Uzbekistan, witnesses said. Guards were not permitting any movement in the opposition direction.
A diplomat at the Afghan consulate in Termez said the office, which represents the administration ousted from the Afghan capital Kabul by the Taleban last year, had stopped issuing visas.
"The situation in Afghanistan is so unclear that we cannot take any risks," he told Reuters.
A concrete barricade blocks the Friendship Bridge, which carried an invading Soviet army into Afghanistan in 1979 -- and back out again, defeated, 10 years later.

Despite a reverse on Wednesday for the Taleban after they were driven out of the northern city of Mazar-i-Sharif, the fighting has raised concern in the region that trouble could spill over into the mainly Moslem ex-Soviet republics of Tajikistan and Uzbekistan.
Tajiks and Uzbeks form considerable ethnic groups in northern Afghanistan and many of them fought the Taleban forces.
On the much longer Tajik-Afghan border to the east, patrolled by Russian forces, the fighting has not increased tensions, a top Russian border guard official said on Wednesday.

"We have not seen a worsening of the situation along the Tajik-Afghan border in connection with recent events in Afghanistan," Aleksei Shcherbakov, deputy director of Russia's federal border service, told a news conference in Moscow.
Some groups of refugees have gathered near the border, he said, but he described their numbers as insignificant.
About 20,000 Russian troops guard the Tajikistan-Afghan border under an agreement with the Tajik government.
The head of Russia's border guards, Andrei Nikolayev, said last month that as many as 100,000 Afghan refugees were gathered near the border with Tajikistan seeking to flee the Taleban.

His deputy, speaking at a news conference, said his forces were ready. "Of course we do not rule out that events could worsen," Shcherbakov said. "In connection with this we are taking preventative measures within our competence."
"But we cannot bar the crossing of refugees from Afghanistan if the situation worsens. However, we have not seen that happening, other than in a few instances," he added.
Russia warned the Taleban on Tuesday it would respond to any breach of the old Soviet-Afghan frontier.
A foreign policy aide to Russian President Boris Yeltsin, Sergei Prikhodko, was cited by Interfax news agency as saying Yeltsin was being informed daily of events in Afghanistan.
Prikhodko said the turbulence was Afghanistan's "internal affair" but said Russia was concerned that fighting might destabilise the rest of the region.
